items.note: Bahadur Shah assigns Bhilsa (perhaps) to Salhadi in jagir.
Bahadur Shah at Bhilsa (1531-32) sacked the city, destroyed temples and built mosques.
Qadir Shah gave eastern Malwa, perhaps including Bhilsa, to Puranmal.
Raisen, Bhilsa and Chanderi remained under Puranmal after Sher Shah's occupation of Malwa.
Sher Shah's advance from Chanderi to Bhilsa in 1543.
Shujaat Khan holds a jagir including Vidisha (Bhilsa); sons placed in charge of Raisen and Bhilsa.
Baz Bahadur takes Raisen and Bhilsa forts and the territory of present Raisen and Vidisha districts.

items.note: Under Akbar, Bhilsa a mahal of Raisen Sarkar: revenue 6,094,970 Dams, 480 horsemen and 1000 infantry.
Aurangzeb destroyed temples of Bhilsa in 1682 including the Vijay Mandir; built a mosque; renamed the town Alamgirpur.
Dost Muhammad Khan of Bhopal moves against Vidisha after Aurangzeb's death.
Dost Muhammad takes Vidisha fort by fraud and becomes master of Gyaraspur and surrounding territories.
Sawai Jai Singh grants Bhilsa to the Nawab of Bhopal; passes to the Marathas.
Vidisha under Maratha administrative control; besieged and taken 11 January 1737.
Marathas take Vidisha fort in 1745; Bhopal obtains Bhilsa fort in 1753; Marathas reoccupy it.
Vidisha tract passes repeatedly between Marathas and Bhopal after Panipat.
Affairs of Vidisha in Sindhia's hands by 1775; part of the former Gwalior State.

items.note: Vidisha region a scene of rebel activity in 1858.
Rebels capture fort of Pipria under Vidisha, 1859; British detachment from Sironj to Sanchi.
After the Revolt Vidisha District, divided among Sindhia, Kurwai, Tonk, Pathari, Muhammadgarh and Basoda, saw no change in ruling houses.
Succession at Basoda in 1864.
Sarvajanik Sabha in Gwalior State (1929); attempted Praja Mandal at Vidisha refused by Gwalior Government.
1948 responsible government in Gwalior; present Vidisha District (except Sironj) part of Madhya Bharat.
1956 reorganisation: Sironj and Lateri become tahsils of Vidisha District.
1971 Census: district population 658,427; four towns and 1,510 villages; density 89.
1901 pargana populations of Bhilsa (54,293) and Basoda (65,896); population nearly trebled 1901-71.
District's rich black cotton soil gives considerable power of quick recuperation.
1931 population fall described as peculiar; seasonal labour influx explains 1921 rise.
District growth 26.71 per cent (1951-61) and 34.59 per cent (1961-71).
